title: Integrated Rate Equations (Zero & First-Order Rate Laws, Half-Life Periods)
syllabus: Integrated rate equations for zero-order reactions ([A] = [A]0 - kt, x = kt); Half-life period of a zero-order reaction (t1/2 = [A]0 / 2k); Graphical representations for zero-order kinetics ([A] vs t, rate vs [A], t1/2 vs [A]0); Integrated rate equations for first-order reactions (k = (2.303/t) log([A]0/[A]), [A] = [A]0 e^(-kt)); Half-life of first-order reactions (t1/2 = 0.693/k, independence of initial concentration); Graphical representations for first-order kinetics (log[A] vs t, ln[A] vs t, [A] vs t, t1/2 vs [A]0); Fractional life periods (t75%, t87.5%, t99%, t99.9% relationships); First-order gas-phase reactions in a closed vessel (k = (2.303/t) log(Pi / (2Pi - Pt))); Radioactive decay as a first-order kinetic process (decay constant, average life τ = 1/k = 1.44 t1/2); General formula for nth order half-life (t1/2 ∝ 1 / [A]0^(n-1)); Numerical problem-solving and graphical interpretation tailored to NEET

questions.question: [NEET 2023] A first-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 4.606 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The time required for $2.0\text{ g}$ of the reactant to be reduced to $0.2\text{ g}$ is:
questions.solution:
1. Using the integrated first-order rate equation:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}\right)$$
2. Substitute the given values:
- $[A]_0 = 2.0\text{ g}$
- $[A] = 0.2\text{ g}$
- $k = 4.606 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$
$$t = \frac{2.303}{4.606 \times 10^{-3}} \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.0}{0.2}\right)$$
$$t = \frac{10^3}{2} \log_{10}(10) = 500 \times 1 = 500\text{ s}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a first-order reaction, the ratio of the time required to complete $99.9\%$ of the reaction ($t_{99.9\%}$) to its half-life period ($t_{1/2}$) is approximately:

[NEET 2021] A zero-order reaction has an initial concentration of reactant equal to $0.2\text{ M}$ and a rate constant $k = 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The half-life period ($t_{1/2}$) of this reaction is:
questions.solution:
1. For a zero-order reaction, the half-life period is given by:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$$
2. Substitute $[A]_0 = 0.2\text{ M}$ and $k = 0.002\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.2}{2 \times 0.002} = \frac{0.2}{0.004} = 50\text{ s}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] Which of the following graphs correctly represents a FIRST-ORDER reaction?
options: A plot of $\ln[A]$ versus time $t$ showing a straight line with negative slope ($-k$) and y-intercept $\ln[A]_0$
A plot of $[A]$ versus time $t$ showing a straight line with negative slope ($-k$)
A plot of $t_{1/2}$ versus initial concentration $[A]_0$ showing a straight line passing through the origin
A plot of $\frac{1}{[A]}$ versus time $t$ showing a straight line with negative slope
questions.solution:
1. The integrated rate law for a first-order reaction is:
$$\ln[A] = \ln[A]_0 - kt$$
Comparing with $y = mx + c$:
- $y = \ln[A]$
- $x = t$
- $\text{Slope } m = -k$ (negative slope)
- $\text{Intercept } c = \ln[A]_0$
Thus, a plot of $\ln[A]$ versus $t$ gives a straight line with negative slope $-k$.
2. Option B corresponds to zero-order kinetics ($[A] = [A]_0 - kt$).
3. Option C corresponds to zero-order kinetics ($t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$). For a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$, which is independent of $[A]_0$ (horizontal line).

questions.question: [NEET 2020] The half-life period of a first-order reaction is $60\text{ minutes}$. What percentage of the reactant will remain unreacted after $240\text{ minutes}$?
questions.solution:
1. Determine the number of half-lives ($n$) elapsed:
$$n = \frac{\text{Total time } (t)}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{240\text{ min}}{60\text{ min}} = 4$$
2. The fraction of reactant remaining after $n$ half-lives is:
$$\frac{[A]}{[A]_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \frac{1}{16}$$
3. Convert to percentage remaining:
$$\% \text{ remaining} = \frac{1}{16} \times 100 = 6.25\%$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a zero-order reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, if the initial concentration is doubled, its half-life period will:
questions.solution:
1. The half-life period of a zero-order reaction is:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$$
2. Since $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0$, the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration.
3. Therefore, doubling the initial concentration of the reactant doubles the half-life period.

questions.question: [NEET 2021] A first-order reaction is $75\%$ complete in $32\text{ minutes}$. The time required for $50\%$ completion ($t_{1/2}$) of the same reaction is:
questions.solution:
1. For a first-order reaction, completing $75\%$ means $25\%$ remains ($[A] = \frac{[A]_0}{4} = \frac{[A]_0}{2^2}$).
2. This corresponds exactly to two consecutive half-lives:
$$t_{75\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$$
3. Given $t_{75\%} = 32\text{ minutes}$:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{t_{75\%}}{2} = \frac{32}{2} = 16\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question:
[NEET 2023] For a gas-phase first-order reaction:
$$A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g) + C(g)$$
Initial pressure of $A$ was $P_i$. If the total pressure of the gas mixture at time $t$ is $P_t$, the integrated rate expression for the rate constant $k$ is:
questions.solution:
1. Set up partial pressures at time $t$:
$$\begin{array}{lccc} & A(g) & \rightarrow 2B(g) & + & C(g) \\ \text{Initial} & P_i & 0 & 0 \\ \text{At time } t & P_i - p & 2p & p \end{array}$$
2. Total pressure at time $t$:
$$P_t = (P_i - p) + 2p + p = P_i + 2p$$
$$2p = P_t - P_i \implies p = \frac{P_t - P_i}{2}$$
3. Remaining partial pressure of reactant $A$ ($P_A$):
$$P_A = P_i - p = P_i - \left(\frac{P_t - P_i}{2}\right) = \frac{2P_i - P_t + P_i}{2} = \frac{3P_i - P_t}{2}$$
4. Using the first-order rate formula:
$$k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\left(\frac{P_i}{P_A}\right) = \frac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\left(\frac{P_i}{\frac{3P_i - P_t}{2}}\right) = \frac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\left(\frac{2P_i}{3P_i - P_t}\right)$$

questions.question: [NEET 2020] The rate constant of a first-order reaction is $k = 6.93 \times 10^{-3}\text{ min}^{-1}$. The time taken for the reactant concentration to fall from $1.0\text{ M}$ to $0.125\text{ M}$ is:
questions.solution:
1. Half-life of the reaction:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} = \frac{0.693}{6.93 \times 10^{-3}\text{ min}^{-1}} = 100\text{ min}$$
2. The concentration decreases from $1.0\text{ M}$ to $0.125\text{ M}$:
$$\frac{[A]}{[A]_0} = \frac{0.125}{1.0} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$$
3. This represents exactly $3$ half-lives:
$$t = 3 \times t_{1/2} = 3 \times 100\text{ min} = 300\text{ min}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a general $n^{\text{th}}$-order chemical reaction ($n \ne 1$), the half-life period ($t_{1/2}$) is related to the initial concentration of reactant ($[A]_0$) by:
questions.solution:
1. For an $n^{\text{th}}$-order reaction, integrating the rate law $-\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k [A]^n$ gives:
$$\frac{1}{[A]^{n-1}} - \frac{1}{[A]_0^{n-1}} = (n - 1)kt$$
2. Setting $[A] = \frac{[A]_0}{2}$ at $t = t_{1/2}$:
$$\frac{2^{n-1} - 1}{[A]_0^{n-1}} = (n - 1)kt_{1/2}$$
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{2^{n-1} - 1}{(n - 1)k [A]_0^{n-1}} \implies t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0^{n-1}}$$
- For $n = 0$: $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0$
- For $n = 1$: $t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0^0$ (independent)
- For $n = 2$: $t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0}$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] Radioactive decay of carbon-$14$ ($^{14}\text{C}$) has a half-life of $5730\text{ years}$. An archaeological wooden sample contains only $25\%$ of the $^{14}\text{C}$ found in fresh living trees. The age of the wooden relic is:
questions.solution:
1. All radioactive decay processes strictly follow first-order kinetics.
2. The sample contains $25\%$ of original $^{14}\text{C}$:
$$\frac{[N]}{[N]_0} = 25\% = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2$$
3. This corresponds to $n = 2$ half-lives.
4. Age of the relic:
$$\text{Age} = n \times t_{1/2} = 2 \times 5730\text{ years} = 11460\text{ years}$$

questions.question: For a zero-order reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, the time required for complete consumption of the reactant ($100\%$ completion) is:
questions.solution:
1. The integrated zero-order equation is:
$$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$
2. For complete consumption ($100\%$ completion), $[A] = 0$:
$$0 = [A]_0 - k t_{100\%} \implies k t_{100\%} = [A]_0 \implies t_{100\%} = \frac{[A]_0}{k}$$
(Notice that $t_{100\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$, meaning a zero-order reaction finishes in finite time, whereas a first-order reaction requires infinite time to reach completion).

questions.question: [NEET 2023] A first-order reaction is $50\%$ complete in $20\text{ minutes}$. How much time will it take to reach $87.5\%$ completion?
questions.solution:
1. When $87.5\%$ of the reactant is consumed, the fraction remaining is:
$$[A] = 100\% - 87.5\% = 12.5\% = \frac{1}{8} [A]_0 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 [A]_0$$
2. Decreasing to $\frac{1}{8}$ of the initial amount takes exactly $3$ half-lives:
$$t_{87.5\%} = 3 \times t_{1/2}$$
3. Given $t_{1/2} = 20\text{ minutes}$:
$$t_{87.5\%} = 3 \times 20\text{ min} = 60\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2020] In a reaction, the concentration of the reactant is reduced from $0.8\text{ M}$ to $0.4\text{ M}$ in $15\text{ minutes}$, and from $0.1\text{ M}$ to $0.05\text{ M}$ in $15\text{ minutes}$. What is the order of the reaction?
questions.solution:
1. In the first instance, concentration drops to half (from $0.8\text{ M}$ to $0.4\text{ M}$) in $15\text{ minutes}$. Hence, $t_{1/2} = 15\text{ min}$.
2. In the second instance, with a different initial concentration ($0.1\text{ M}$), concentration again drops to half ($0.05\text{ M}$) in the exact same time ($15\text{ minutes}$).
3. Because the half-life is constant and completely independent of initial concentration, the reaction must be **first order** ($t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$).

questions.question: [NEET 2022] What is the slope of the linear plot of $\log_{10}[A]$ versus time $t$ for a first-order reaction?
questions.solution:
1. The integrated rate equation in common logarithms (base 10) is:
$$\log_{10}[A] = \log_{10}[A]_0 - \frac{k}{2.303} t$$
2. Comparing with the straight-line equation $y = mx + c$:
- $y = \log_{10}[A]$
- $x = t$
- $\text{Intercept } c = \log_{10}[A]_0$
- $\text{Slope } m = -\frac{k}{2.303}$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] For a first-order reaction $A \rightarrow B$, the rate constant is $k = 0.693\text{ min}^{-1}$. What is the rate of the reaction when $[A] = 0.2\text{ M}$?
questions.solution:
From the differential rate law for a first-order reaction:
$$\text{Rate} = k [A]^1$$
Substitute $k = 0.693\text{ min}^{-1}$ and $[A] = 0.2\text{ M}$:
$$\text{Rate} = 0.693\text{ min}^{-1} \times 0.2\text{ mol L}^{-1} = 0.1386\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] If a first-order reaction takes $40\text{ minutes}$ to achieve $90\%$ completion, its half-life period ($t_{1/2}$) is: (Take $\log_{10} 2 = 0.301$)
[NEET 2020] The average life (mean life, $\tau$) of a first-order reaction is related to its half-life ($t_{1/2}$) by:
questions.solution:
1. Average life ($\tau$) is defined as the reciprocal of the rate constant (or decay constant):
$$\tau = \frac{1}{k}$$
2. Since $t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693}{k}$, we have $k = \frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$.
3. Substitute $k$ into the expression for $\tau$:
$$\tau = \frac{1}{0.693 / t_{1/2}} = \frac{t_{1/2}}{0.693} \approx 1.443\, t_{1/2}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a zero-order reaction, the slope of the plot of reactant concentration $[A]$ versus time $t$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
1. The integrated rate equation for zero-order kinetics is:
$$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$
2. Comparing with $y = mx + c$:
- $y = [A]$
- $x = t$
- $c = [A]_0$
- $\text{Slope } m = -k$
Therefore, the slope is $-k$.

questions.question: [NEET 2021] In a first-order reaction $A \rightarrow \text{Products}$, $[A]_0 = 0.1\text{ M}$. After $40\text{ minutes}$, the concentration is $0.025\text{ M}$. The rate of reaction when $[A] = 0.01\text{ M}$ is:
questions.solution:
1. Notice that $[A]$ drops from $0.1\text{ M}$ to $0.025\text{ M}$:
$$\frac{[A]}{[A]_0} = \frac{0.025}{0.1} = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2$$
This corresponds to $2$ half-lives in $40\text{ minutes}$:
$$2 \times t_{1/2} = 40\text{ min} \implies t_{1/2} = 20\text{ min}$$
2. Find rate constant $k$:
$$k = \frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{20\text{ min}} = 0.03465\text{ min}^{-1}$$
3. Calculate rate when $[A] = 0.01\text{ M}$:
$$\text{Rate} = k [A] = 0.03465\text{ min}^{-1} \times 0.01\text{ M} = 3.465 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M min}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] A vessel contains a gas-phase first-order reaction $A(g) \rightarrow B(g) + C(g)$. The initial pressure was $80\text{ mm Hg}$. After $10\text{ minutes}$, the total pressure rose to $120\text{ mm Hg}$. What is the rate constant $k$ of the reaction? (Take $\ln 2 = 0.693$)
questions.solution:
1. Let partial pressure decrease by $p$:
- $P_A = 80 - p$
- $P_B = p$
- $P_C = p$
$$P_{\text{total}} = 80 - p + p + p = 80 + p = 120\text{ mm Hg} \implies p = 40\text{ mm Hg}$$
2. Remaining pressure of $A$:
$$P_A = 80 - 40 = 40\text{ mm Hg}$$
3. Since $P_A$ fell from $80\text{ mm Hg}$ to $40\text{ mm Hg}$ (half of initial) in $10\text{ minutes}$, the half-life is $t_{1/2} = 10\text{ min}$.
4. Calculate $k$:
$$k = \frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{10\text{ min}} = 0.0693\text{ min}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
[NEET 2020] For a reaction, the half-life period was measured for different initial concentrations:

- When $[A]_0 = 0.1\text{ M}$, $t_{1/2} = 200\text{ s}$
- When $[A]_0 = 0.4\text{ M}$, $t_{1/2} = 50\text{ s}$

The order of the reaction is:
questions.solution:
1. Use the proportional relationship for half-life:
$$t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0^{n - 1}}$$
$$\frac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \left(\frac{[A]_{0,2}}{[A]_{0,1}}\right)^{n - 1}$$
2. Substitute the values:
$$\frac{200}{50} = \left(\frac{0.4}{0.1}\right)^{n - 1}$$
$$4 = 4^{n - 1} \implies 4^1 = 4^{n - 1}$$
$$n - 1 = 1 \implies n = 2$$
Therefore, the reaction is of **second order**.

questions.question: [NEET 2022] A substance decomposes following first-order kinetics with $k = 1.386 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. How long will it take for the concentration to fall to $1/16^{\text{th}}$ of its initial value?
questions.solution:
1. Half-life:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} = \frac{0.693}{1.386 \times 10^{-2}} = \frac{0.693}{0.01386} = 50\text{ s}$$
2. Falling to $\frac{1}{16} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4$ takes $4$ half-lives:
$$t = 4 \times t_{1/2} = 4 \times 50\text{ s} = 200\text{ s}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] For a first-order reaction, the time required to complete $99\%$ of the reaction ($t_{99\%}$) is related to the time required to complete $90\%$ of the reaction ($t_{90\%}$) by:
[NEET 2023] A zero-order reaction is $20\%$ complete in $20\text{ seconds}$. How long will it take to reach $80\%$ completion?
questions.solution:
1. In zero-order kinetics, the amount of reactant converted ($x$) is directly proportional to time:
$$x = kt \implies t \propto x$$
2. Set up the proportion:
$$\frac{t_2}{t_1} = \frac{x_2}{x_1}$$
Given $x_1 = 20\%$, $t_1 = 20\text{ s}$, and $x_2 = 80\%$:
$$\frac{t_2}{20} = \frac{80}{20} = 4$$
$$t_2 = 4 \times 20 = 80\text{ seconds}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2020] Which of the following statements about a first-order reaction is INCORRECT?
options: The time required for $100\%$ completion is equal to $2 \times t_{1/2}$
The half-life period is independent of initial concentration
The rate constant has units of $\text{time}^{-1}$
A plot of $[A]$ versus time shows an exponential decay curve
questions.solution:
1. For a first-order reaction, the concentration decreases exponentially according to $[A] = [A]_0 e^{-kt}$.
2. The concentration approaches zero only as time approaches infinity ($t \rightarrow \infty$). Therefore, a first-order reaction **never goes to $100\%$ completion in finite time**.
3. ($t_{100\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$ is true for a *zero-order* reaction, not a first-order reaction).
Hence, Statement A is incorrect.

questions.question: [NEET 2022] In a first-order reaction, the reactant concentration drops from $0.6\text{ M}$ to $0.3\text{ M}$ in $20\text{ minutes}$, and from $0.3\text{ M}$ to $0.15\text{ M}$ in another $20\text{ minutes}$. What is the value of the rate constant $k$?
questions.solution:
1. In both intervals, the concentration is halved in $20\text{ minutes}$, so the half-life is $t_{1/2} = 20\text{ min}$.
2. For first-order kinetics:
$$k = \frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{20\text{ min}} = 0.03465\text{ min}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] What fraction of a radioactive substance remains undecayed after a time interval equal to $5$ half-lives?
questions.solution:
After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is:
$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$
For $n = 5$:
$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 = \frac{1}{32}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] In an experiment on the decomposition of $A$, a straight-line plot was obtained when $[A]$ was plotted against time $t$. The rate constant of this reaction is equal to:
questions.solution:
1. A linear plot of $[A]$ versus $t$ is the hallmark of a **zero-order reaction**:
$$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$
2. Comparing with $y = mx + c$:
$$\text{Slope } m = -k \implies k = -m = -(\text{slope})$$

questions.question: [NEET 2020] A first-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$ with an initial reactant concentration of $0.5\text{ M}$. What is the half-life period of the reaction?
questions.solution:
1. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is independent of the initial concentration ($[A]_0 = 0.5\text{ M}$ is extra information):
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$$
2. Substitute $k = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 693\text{ s}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a zero-order reaction, if the rate constant is $k = 0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$ and $[A]_0 = 1.0\text{ M}$, what is the concentration of $A$ remaining after $15\text{ seconds}$?
questions.solution:
Using the zero-order integrated equation:
$$[A] = [A]_0 - kt$$
Substitute $[A]_0 = 1.0\text{ M}$, $k = 0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$, and $t = 15\text{ s}$:
$$[A] = 1.0 - (0.05 \times 15) = 1.0 - 0.75 = 0.25\text{ M}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] A first-order reaction has $t_{1/2} = 10\text{ minutes}$. What is the time required to complete $99.6\%$ of the reaction? (Take $\log_{10} 2 = 0.301$)
questions.solution:
1. When $99.6\%$ is complete, the remaining fraction is:
$$[A] = 100\% - 99.6\% = 0.4\% = 0.004 [A]_0 = \frac{4}{1000} [A]_0 = \frac{1}{250} [A]_0$$
Notice that $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^8 = \frac{1}{256} \approx \frac{1}{250}$ (or $0.39\%$ remaining $\approx 99.6\%$ completion).
2. This represents approximately $8$ half-lives:
$$t = 8 \times t_{1/2} = 8 \times 10\text{ min} = 80\text{ minutes}$$
3. (Exact formula: $t = \frac{2.303 \times 10}{0.693} \log_{10}(250) = 33.23 \times 2.398 \approx 79.7\text{ min} \approx 80\text{ min}$).

questions.question: [NEET 2023] Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the half-life period of a chemical reaction?
options: For a zero-order reaction, $t_{1/2}$ is directly proportional to initial concentration; for a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2}$ is independent of initial concentration
For a zero-order reaction, $t_{1/2}$ is inversely proportional to initial concentration
For a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2}$ is directly proportional to initial concentration
For all reactions, $t_{1/2}$ is independent of initial concentration
questions.solution:
1. For zero-order: $t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} \implies t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0$ (directly proportional).
2. For first-order: $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} \implies t_{1/2} \propto [A]_0^0$ (strictly independent of $[A]_0$).
3. For second-order: $t_{1/2} = \frac{1}{k[A]_0} \implies t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{[A]_0}$ (inversely proportional).
Therefore, Statement A is correct.

questions.question: [NEET 2020] A first-order reaction is $50\%$ complete in $1.26 \times 10^{14}\text{ s}$. How much time will it take to reach $100\%$ completion?
questions.solution:
1. The integrated rate law for first-order kinetics is:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}\right)$$
2. For $100\%$ completion, $[A] = 0$:
$$t_{100\%} = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{0}\right) = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10}(\infty) = \infty$$
3. A first-order reaction decays exponentially and theoretically takes an infinite amount of time to reach zero concentration.

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a zero-order reaction, the time required for the initial concentration $[A]_0$ to reduce to one-fourth ($25\%$) of its initial value is:
[NEET 2021] Two first-order reactions have rate constants $k_1$ and $k_2$. If $k_1 = 2 k_2$, the ratio of their half-life periods $(t_{1/2})_1 / (t_{1/2})_2$ is:
questions.solution:
1. For a first-order reaction:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} \implies t_{1/2} \propto \frac{1}{k}$$
2. Taking the ratio:
$$\frac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \frac{k_2}{k_1}$$
3. Given $k_1 = 2 k_2$:
$$\frac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \frac{k_2}{2 k_2} = \frac{1}{2} = 1 : 2$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] In a first-order reaction, the time required to complete $75\%$ of the reaction is $t_1$, and the time required to complete $50\%$ is $t_2$. The relation between $t_1$ and $t_2$ is:
questions.solution:
1. $t_2$ is the half-life ($t_{1/2}$), the time for $50\%$ completion:
$$t_2 = \frac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}(2)$$
2. $t_1$ is the time for $75\%$ completion (leaving $25\% = 1/4$):
$$t_1 = \frac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}(4) = \frac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}(2^2) = 2 \times \frac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}(2) = 2 t_2$$
Thus, $t_1 = 2 t_2$.

questions.question: [NEET 2020] A sample of radioactive isotope undergoes decay. If the activity of the sample decreases to $10\%$ of its initial activity in $23.03\text{ days}$, the decay constant ($\lambda$) is:
questions.solution:
1. Radioactive decay obeys first-order kinetics:
$$\lambda = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10}\left(\frac{A_0}{A}\right)$$
2. Given $\frac{A}{A_0} = 10\% = 0.10 \implies \frac{A_0}{A} = 10$, and $t = 23.03\text{ days}$:
$$\lambda = \frac{2.303}{23.03} \log_{10}(10) = 0.10 \times 1 = 0.10\text{ day}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a zero-order reaction, which of the following expressions correctly relates the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) to the rate constant ($k$)?
questions.solution:
1. For a zero-order reaction: $t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$.
2. Rearranging for $k$:
$$k = \frac{[A]_0}{2 t_{1/2}}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2021] A first-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 2.303 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. How long will it take for the concentration of the reactant to reduce to $1/10^{\text{th}}$ of its initial value?
questions.solution:
1. Using the integrated first-order rate law:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}\right)$$
2. Substitute $[A] = \frac{[A]_0}{10} \implies \frac{[A]_0}{[A]} = 10$, and $k = 2.303 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$:
$$t = \frac{2.303}{2.303 \times 10^{-2}} \log_{10}(10) = 10^2 \times 1 = 100\text{ s}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] If the rate constant of a reaction has the numerical value $k = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$, what is the order of the reaction?
questions.solution:
1. The unit of the rate constant is given as $\text{s}^{-1}$ (or $\text{time}^{-1}$).
2. From the dimensional formula $\text{mol}^{1-n}\text{ L}^{n-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$, the concentration terms disappear only when:
$$1 - n = 0 \implies n = 1$$
Therefore, any rate constant with the unit of reciprocal time ($\text{s}^{-1}, \text{min}^{-1}, \text{hr}^{-1}$) corresponds exclusively to a **first-order reaction**.

questions.question: [NEET 2020] For a first-order reaction $A \rightarrow B$, the plot of $\log_{10}[A]$ against time $t$ gives a straight line with a slope of $-0.03\text{ s}^{-1}$. The rate constant ($k$) of the reaction is: (Take $2.303 \times 0.03 \approx 0.069\text{ s}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
1. The slope of the $\log_{10}[A]$ vs $t$ plot is:
$$\text{Slope} = -\frac{k}{2.303}$$
2. Given $\text{slope} = -0.03\text{ s}^{-1}$:
$$-\frac{k}{2.303} = -0.03$$
$$k = 0.03 \times 2.303 = 0.06909\text{ s}^{-1} \approx 0.069\text{ s}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2022] For a first-order reaction, the ratio of $t_{75\%}$ to $t_{50\%}$ is $2$. What is the ratio of $t_{87.5\%}$ to $t_{50\%}$?
[NEET 2021] A zero-order reaction has a rate constant $k = 0.1\text{ M min}^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of reactant is $2.0\text{ M}$, what is its half-life period?
questions.solution:
Using the zero-order half-life equation:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k} = \frac{2.0\text{ M}}{2 \times 0.1\text{ M min}^{-1}} = \frac{2.0}{0.2} = 10\text{ minutes}$$

questions.question: [NEET 2023] An organic compound decomposes by first-order kinetics. In an experiment, it was observed that $60\%$ of the compound decomposes in $60\text{ minutes}$. What percentage of the compound remains unreacted after $120\text{ minutes}$?
questions.solution:
1. In the first $60\text{ minutes}$, $60\%$ decomposed, meaning $40\%$ remained unreacted:
$$\frac{[A]_{60}}{[A]_0} = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40$$
2. In first-order kinetics, the fraction of reactant remaining in any constant time interval is identical.
3. In the second $60\text{ minute}$ interval (from $60$ to $120\text{ minutes}$), $40\%$ of the concentration present at $60\text{ minutes}$ remains:
$$[A]_{120} = 0.40 \times [A]_{60} = 0.40 \times (0.40 [A]_0) = 0.16 [A]_0$$
4. Percentage remaining after $120\text{ minutes}$:
$$\% \text{ remaining} = 0.16 \times 100 = 16\%$$
